passed.title: Series.round uses bankers' rounding by default, not half-up
passed.trap: `Series.round` defaults to `mode='half_to_even'`, so a value exactly halfway between two candidates goes to the even one: 0.5 becomes 0.0 and 2.5 becomes 2.0. SQL `ROUND` and spreadsheet users usually expect half away from zero, so totals and labels can silently differ. Pass `mode='half_away_from_zero'` when you need that behaviour.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

s = pl.Series("x", [0.5, 1.5, 2.5, -2.5])

# Default: half_to_even (bankers' rounding)
print(s.round().to_list())  # [0.0, 2.0, 2.0, -2.0]

# SQL-style rounding
print(s.round(mode="half_away_from_zero").to_list())  # [1.0, 2.0, 3.0, -3.0]

passed.title: Series.sum returns 0, not None, when there are no non-null values
passed.trap: `Series.sum` on an empty or all-null Series returns `0`, not `None` or null. Code that checks `if total is None` to detect missing data will never fire. If an empty sum should be `None`, use `s.sum() if s.count() else None` as the docstring suggests. Note also that Int8/UInt8/Int16/UInt16 are cast to Int64 before summing, so the result does not overflow the small dtype.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

all_null = pl.Series("x", [None, None], dtype=pl.Int64)
print(all_null.sum())  # 0, not None

# Explicitly treat 'no data' as None
print(all_null.sum() if all_null.count() else None)  # None

# Small ints are widened before summing, so no overflow
small = pl.Series("y", [100, 100], dtype=pl.Int8)
print(small.sum())  # 200

passed.title: Series.sort puts nulls first and returns a new Series
passed.trap: `Series.sort` defaults to `nulls_last=False`, so nulls come first. This also applies with `descending=True`. pandas users expect nulls at the end (`na_position='last'`), so taking the first element after a sort may give you a null. Pass `nulls_last=True` explicitly. The call also returns a new Series (`in_place=False`), so calling `s.sort()` without assigning the result leaves `s` unchanged.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

s = pl.Series("x", [3, None, 1])

print(s.sort().to_list())                 # [None, 1, 3]
print(s.sort(descending=True).to_list())  # [None, 3, 1]
print(s.sort(nulls_last=True).to_list())  # [1, 3, None]

s.sort()  # result discarded
print(s.to_list())  # [3, None, 1] -- unchanged

s = s.sort(nulls_last=True)
print(s.to_list())  # [1, 3, None]

passed.title: Series.skew is biased by default, unlike pandas
passed.trap: `Series.skew` defaults to `bias=True` and returns the plain Fisher-Pearson coefficient g1. pandas `skew()` returns the bias-adjusted G1, so porting code gives a different number on small samples. Pass `bias=False` to get the adjusted coefficient.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

s = pl.Series([1, 2, 2, 4, 5])

biased = s.skew()               # default bias=True -> g1
adjusted = s.skew(bias=False)   # adjusted G1 (pandas-style)

print(round(biased, 6))    # 0.347767
print(round(adjusted, 6))  # larger value
print(biased == adjusted)  # False

passed.title: Series.slice takes a length, not a stop index
passed.trap: `Series.slice(offset, length)` takes a start and a number of elements. It is not Python's `[start:stop]`. Calling `s.slice(1, 3)` returns three elements starting at index 1, not indices 1 and 2. Compute `length = stop - start` when translating slicing code. With `Series.tail`, a negative `n` returns everything except the first `abs(n)` elements; it does not count back from the end.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

s = pl.Series("a", [10, 20, 30, 40, 50])

print(s.slice(1, 3).to_list())      # [20, 30, 40] -- 3 elements, not stop=3

start, stop = 1, 3
print(s.slice(start, stop - start).to_list())  # [20, 30] == python s[1:3]

print(s.slice(-2).to_list())        # [40, 50]
print(s.tail(-2).to_list())         # [30, 40, 50] -- all except first 2

passed.title: Series.set_sorted on unsorted data silently gives wrong answers
passed.trap: `Series.set_sorted` does not sort or check anything. It only sets a flag that later operations trust for fast paths. If the data is not actually sorted, aggregations such as `Series.max` can return wrong values with no error. Use `Series.sort` unless you are certain the data is already ordered.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

s = pl.Series("a", [3, 1, 2])

flagged = s.set_sorted()  # lies: data is not sorted
print(flagged.max())      # may be wrong (fast path returns the last value)

print(s.max())            # 3 -- correct
print(s.sort().max())     # 3 -- sort for real instead of flagging

passed.title: Series.rolling_var returns null for any window containing a null
passed.trap: For `Series.rolling_var`, `min_samples=None` means it is set to `window_size`. As a result, a single null inside a window makes that row's result null, not just the first `window_size - 1` rows. Lower `min_samples` to compute variance over the available values. The parameter was renamed from `min_periods` in 1.21.0, so use `min_samples`. By contrast, the unstable `Series.rolling_var_by` defaults to `min_samples=1`, and its windows default to `closed='right'`. Both use `ddof=1`.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

s = pl.Series("a", [1.0, None, 3.0, 4.0, 5.0])

# Default min_samples == window_size: one null kills 3 windows
print(s.rolling_var(3).round(6).to_list())
# [None, None, None, None, 1.0]

# Allow windows with at least 2 non-null values
print(s.rolling_var(3, min_samples=2).round(6).to_list())
# [None, None, 2.0, 0.5, 1.0]

passed.title: Pass side explicitly to Series.search_sorted when there are duplicates
passed.trap: `Series.search_sorted` defaults to `side='any'`, which returns the first suitable location the search finds. With duplicate values, that is not documented to be the leftmost one. Use `side='left'` or `side='right'` when you need `bisect_left` or `bisect_right` semantics. The Series must already be sorted; pass `descending=True` if it is sorted descending. The return type depends on the input: a scalar returns a Python `int`, and a list returns a `Series`.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

s = pl.Series("vals", [1, 2, 3, 4, 4, 5, 6, 7])

print(s.search_sorted(4, side="left"))   # 3 (bisect_left)
print(s.search_sorted(4, side="right"))  # 5 (bisect_right)

scalar = s.search_sorted(4, side="left")
many = s.search_sorted([1, 4, 5], side="left")
print(isinstance(scalar, int))        # True
print(isinstance(many, pl.Series))    # True
print(many.to_list())                 # [0, 3, 5]

The output shows `0` for an all-null sum and `200` for Int8, matching the docstring notes on empty sums and small-int widening.
The output confirms nulls come first even with `descending=True`, and that discarding the result leaves `s` unchanged.
The output shows the default g1 (0.347767) differs from the `bias=False` G1 (0.518421), consistent with the docstring formulas.
The output confirms that `slice(1, 3)` returns three elements and that `tail(-2)` drops the first two, as documented.
The output shows `max()` returning 2 on a falsely flagged unsorted Series, matching the docstring warning.
The output shows one null nulling every window that contains it, and the `rolling_var_by` defaults and `ddof` claims match the signatures.
